client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup about a month ago. The hours are just brutal — I'm staying late almost every night, and by the time I get home I'm so exhausted I can barely think straight. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there tomorrow no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the exhaustion is real, and it makes sense that part of you wonders what talking can even do when the demands don't just disappear. I also notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something in your voice that feels a bit more strained than your words alone might suggest, like maybe the weight of it is even bigger than you're letting on. What would it mean for you if this conversation *could* actually help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I guess it would mean I'd feel a little less alone in it, which sounds kind of pathetic when I say it out loud. Like, I know logically that other people have hard jobs and they manage, so I feel guilty even complaining about it. But yeah, you're right that it's bigger than I'm making it sound — I've been waking up at 3am just dreading the next day, and I haven't told anyone that until right now.
therapist: Wanting to feel less alone is not pathetic at all — it's one of the most deeply human needs there is, and it takes real courage to say that out loud, especially for the first time. I want to gently push back on that thought that you *should* just manage because others do — comparing your struggle to others' doesn't make yours any less real or deserving of care. Those 3am wake-ups tell me your mind and body are genuinely overwhelmed — what do you think is running through your head in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Usually it's this spiral of like, did I miss something today, is my manager going to think I'm not cut out for this, and then it just snowballs from there. I start mentally rehearsing conversations that haven't even happened yet, like I'm bracing for some kind of disaster. And then I lie there feeling stupid for not being able to just turn my brain off and sleep like a normal person.
therapist: That spiral you're describing — scanning for mistakes, rehearsing imaginary confrontations, bracing for the worst — is actually a really common anxiety pattern, and it makes complete sense your brain is doing it, even though it's exhausting. What strikes me is that underneath all of that mental rehearsing, there seems to be a core fear about not being "cut out for this" — and I'm curious, is that a new fear this job has brought up, or does it feel familiar from other parts of your life too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's definitely not new, if I'm being honest — I've felt like I was one mistake away from being "found out" for most of my adult life, like at any moment people are going to realize I don't actually know what I'm doing. This job just turned the volume up on it way louder than usual. I guess I thought I'd outgrow it by now, and the fact that I haven't makes me feel kind of embarrassed.
therapist: What you're describing has a name — it's called impostor syndrome, and the fact that it's followed you across different stages of your life actually tells us something important: this isn't about your actual competence, it's a deeply ingrained story your mind has been telling you for a long time. I also notice you said all of that quite quickly, like you wanted to get it out before second-guessing yourself — which makes me wonder if even naming it feels a little vulnerable or risky. What do you imagine would happen if the people around you *didn't* eventually "find you out"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's a weird question to sit with, because my honest first reaction is almost like... relief, but then immediately after that comes this feeling of "well, that can't actually happen." Like some part of me genuinely doesn't believe it's possible that I could just be seen as competent and that would be the end of it. I think I'd almost be waiting for the other shoe to drop even then, which I realize sounds exhausting when I say it out loud.
therapist: That flash of relief you noticed is really worth holding onto — it means some part of you *can* imagine a different reality, even if another part rushes in quickly to shut it down. What you're describing, that constant waiting for the other shoe to drop even in good moments, is actually one of the most tiring things about this pattern — there's no finish line where you finally get to feel safe. I'm curious, when did you first learn that good things needed to be braced against, that it wasn't safe to just let them land?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's making me think about growing up, where things at home were pretty unpredictable — like, a good day could turn bad really fast depending on my dad's mood, so I think I just learned to never fully relax even when things seemed okay. I've never really connected that to what's happening now at work, and I'm not sure how I feel about making that link because it almost makes it feel bigger and harder to fix. Like, if this goes back that far, what am I even supposed to do with that?
therapist: You just made a really significant connection, and it makes sense that it feels a bit overwhelming — recognizing that something goes back to childhood can make it feel like the ground shifted under you. But I want to offer a reframe: the fact that this pattern has such deep roots doesn't make it harder to change, it actually helps explain *why* it's been so persistent and why you've worked so hard just to get through each day. This isn't a life sentence — it's actually the beginning of understanding what we're working with, and that's a hopeful place to be.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I want to believe that reframe, I really do, but part of me is skeptical because I've been this way for so long that "hopeful" feels like a stretch right now. Like, okay, so now I understand where it comes from — but I still have to go into that office tomorrow and face the same pressure, and understanding the root of it doesn't make my manager less intimidating or the deadlines less real. I guess I'm just not sure how insight actually translates into feeling different in those moments.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and honestly it would be strange if you *didn't* feel that way — insight alone isn't the finish line, it's more like turning on a light in a room you've been navigating in the dark. The real work is what we build from here: concrete ways to interrupt that spiral in the moment, so that when you're sitting across from your manager, you have something to reach for besides bracing for disaster. Can you think of one specific moment at work — maybe a recent one — where that fear of being "found out" really spiked, so we can start to look at what was actually happening versus what your mind was telling you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: There was this moment last week where my manager asked me to stay after a team meeting, and before he even said a word my heart was already pounding and I was mentally preparing my defense for getting fired. He actually just wanted to ask if I could take on a small extra project because he thought I'd be good at it, and instead of feeling good about that I spent the rest of the day convinced he was setting me up to fail. I know that's not a rational response, but in the moment it felt completely real.
therapist: This is such a perfect example of what we've been talking about — your manager essentially handed you evidence that he sees your competence, and your mind immediately worked to neutralize it by turning it into a threat. That's the pattern in action: good things can't just land safely, they have to be braced against. What do you think it would have taken in that moment to let his confidence in you be *real*, even just for a few minutes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I don't know what it would have taken, because in that moment my body was already in full alarm mode before my brain even had a chance to catch up. Maybe if I'd had some way to pause and actually notice what was happening instead of just being swept along by it — but that feels easier said than done when the adrenaline is already going. I guess I'm wondering if that kind of pause is even something you can actually learn, or if it's just advice that sounds good in a therapy room but falls apart in real life.
therapist: That pause absolutely can be learned — it's actually one of the most well-researched skills in CBT, and what you're describing, that gap between the body's alarm and the mind catching up, is precisely where we'd practice creating just a sliver of space. I notice you're asking this in a way that sounds almost cautious, like you're genuinely curious but also protecting yourself from getting your hopes up again — which makes a lot of sense given everything you've shared today. What if we tried mapping out exactly what that pause could look like for *you*, starting with that moment outside the meeting room, so it feels less like advice and more like something that actually fits your life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Okay, I'm willing to try mapping it out, but I want to be upfront that I'm a little worried it's going to feel too mechanical or scripted when I'm actually standing there with my heart pounding. Like, am I supposed to stop and do breathing exercises in the hallway outside a meeting room at a startup where everyone's already watching to see if you can handle the pace? I guess I just need it to be something that doesn't make me look like I'm falling apart while I'm trying not to fall apart.
therapist: That's such a fair and practical concern, and I want you to know we're not going to build something that requires you to visibly tap out in the middle of a startup hallway. What we're actually aiming for is something almost invisible — a single internal anchor, like a quiet word or a micro-shift in attention, that only you would even notice you're doing. What's one tiny thing that has ever helped you feel even slightly more grounded in a high-pressure moment, even if it seems too small to count?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
